extracted.intended_audience: scholars of political communication and journalists interested in social media use
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and qualities that make political leaders' tweets useful, influential, or newsworthy to political journalists; focused on how tweets function as information subsidies and shape agenda building. Useful for researchers studying social media-journalism interactions and for practitioners crafting tweets for media impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source type / origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Think tanks and interest groups (and political bloggers) are seen as the most useful sources; tweets of elected officials and candidates rated lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants described think tanks and interest groups as 'more about analyzing issues as opposed to telling me what the news of the day is' and noted that these groups 'tweet links to their analyses, which are sometimes useful'. Political bloggers can provide 'mini-scoops' and specialized analysis (e.g., Politico, RealClearPolitics, TNR, ScotusBlog) that are great sources of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / speed / breaking news
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets with news values such as timeliness and breaking-news capability stand out to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter is described as 'possibly the ultimate breaking news tool'; journalists pick up 'ideas, breaking news tips, even press statements from Twitter'. Speed makes tweets useful 'on deadline' for immediate reactions (e.g., instant reactions to a Supreme Court decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-idea generation / tip sheet function
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that spark story ideas or serve as tip sheets are valuable for generating coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants noted that leaders' tweets act as story idea generators and tip sheets; a political tweet acting as a tip sheet influences object salience in coverage (first-level agenda building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to augment existing stories / topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that contain information supplementing an existing story being worked on — topical content — are likely to shape coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: local candidates tweeting about outreach/fundraising provide 'nuggets of news' reporters cover (e.g., how much each candidate has raised). Maria: 'A lot of it is topical.' Such tweets add to broader news stories and match traditional newsworthiness criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of quotes and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that supply quotable material or data (including poll results) are useful sources for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes on Twitter give 'instant access' to leaders not always available for interview (example: Newt Gingrich tweeting an answer so reporters could say 'Newt tweeted'). Poll data and quotes can also shape the attributes of stories (second-level agenda building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider perspective / inside information
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets offering an insider's, unvarnished perspective on issues are sought after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawrence: 'I think that’s valuable, where you’re getting a very unvarnished view.' Alan wanted 'a politician who would tweet a committee meeting... the politician’s perspective as to why a bill is being bottled up in committee' — live, in-the-moment perspectives are especially valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, brevity, and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, punchy, to-the-point tweets are more likely to appeal to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robbie: 'I tend to focus on the ones that are short and punchy ... with a quick sentence or a quick description, and then I can click on the link and go on from there.' Tracie: to-the-point tweets are 'helpful to reporters who are, more and more, being stretched in every direction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Links to in-depth analysis / linkability
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that link to deeper analyses, background pieces, or longer content are particularly valuable to newspaper reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maria and Eddy noted think tanks and interest groups 'tweet links to their analyses', and the 'in-depth analyses linked to in the tweets better fit the needs of newspaper reporters.' Linkability allows quick signal with a path to substantial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public distribution vs targeted press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Because tweets are distributed to both journalists and the public, they function differently from press releases and may have greater public influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tweets are likened to YouTube videos, Facebook posts, and blog posts rather than press releases; public exposure can force journalists to cover issues to appear current or to avoid being scooped. Press releases are generally targeted to journalists only, whereas tweets reach a wider audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of sources / ideological breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a wide range of leaders on Twitter exposes journalists to diverse viewpoints and influences what they cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maria makes 'a conscious effort' to expand ideological diversity of whom she follows to avoid perceived bias and to see viewpoints she 'may not have thought about'. Twitter's public environment subtly forces journalists to receive information from a wider range of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility for immediate reactions / 'first draft' quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets provide immediate reactions that can be used for quick-round, deadline-driven coverage (the 'first draft' of statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sydney: Twitter has become the first draft of the '...said in a statement' comment; useful when seeking immediate reactions to events for a first cut of a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as background information and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets serve as resources for background information to understand issues and as fact-checking tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants reported using tweets to help understand issues (background) rather than always appearing word-for-word in stories; tweets can aid fact-checking and issue comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-subsidy characteristics (cost/accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets are free, easily available information subsidies that reduce the cost to journalists of obtaining material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Gandy: information subsidies are 'made available at something less than the cost a user would face in the absence of the subsidy' — tweets are free and easily available, increasing their attractiveness compared to costlier information sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for second-level agenda building (attribute framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets containing quotes and poll data can influence not only what issues are covered but how issues and actors are portrayed (attributes, tone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-level agenda building occurs when information subsidies shape the attributes in journalists' stories that portray issues, candidates, and other objects; the paper notes that quotes and poll data used by journalists have the potential to influence those attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform specificity (Twitter vs Facebook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter is more beneficial for political journalists than Facebook, which is used more for personal life by political actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding matches earlier work: political consultants and politically interested individuals use Facebook for personal life but Twitter 'for politics' (Parmelee and Bichard, 2012), making Twitter the preferred platform for political news sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/beat and location sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of tweets may vary by journalists' beat (TV, health, science, local) and work location (state capitols, Washington), so usefulness is context-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most participants worked in state capitol bureaus and Washington, D.C.; prior research suggested journalists in centers of power are less influenced by political information subsidies, so contextual differences exist and warrant further study. The paper also notes the need to study television and other beats separately.
